DEU.story:
A youth office in Germany is the public body that decides where a child lives when there is no safe home. It has the legal power to choose the foster father, and the family has little say. From the late 1960s the youth authorities in West Berlin used that power to place homeless boys with men they knew were paedophiles. They did it on the advice of a sexologist, Helmut Kentler, and an expert's recommendation is what allows officials to sign something they would otherwise refuse, because responsibility moves to the expert. A University of Hildesheim report in 2024 traced a network across the country that tolerated the arrangement past 2000. Kentler died in 2008 and was never prosecuted.

German law, like most law, sets a deadline for bringing a case: once it passes, no charge can be brought however good the evidence. That turns an institution's delay into a defence. At the Odenwaldschule, a boarding school in Heppenheim, at least 132 pupils were abused between the 1960s and the 1990s, some of them by the headmaster, Gerold Becker. Pupils came forward in 1998 and a newspaper printed the account in 1999. The review the school promised never happened, and when prosecutors finally looked they dropped the case because the time limit had run out. Becker died in 2010 without facing a court. In March 2013 the Bundestag, the national parliament, extended the deadline for suing from three years to thirty and made the criminal clock start only at a victim's twenty-first birthday, but it did not apply the change backwards, so claims that had already expired stayed expired.

The other German habit was to send the man somewhere else, which leaves the complaint in the old place and the priest in a new one where nobody has heard it. Fr Peter Hullermann was reported in Essen in 1979, accepted into Munich in 1980 under Cardinal Ratzinger for therapy, given parish work, and abused again; the first legal action came in 1986. A study the bishops themselves commissioned, published in 2018, counted 1,670 clerics accused of abusing 3,677 minors from 1946 to 2014, and found personnel files destroyed or altered.

Germany shows that the office with the legal power to protect a child is also the office that can hand the child over, and that a long silence is not only a moral failure — in law it can end the case. When a report says a prosecution was dropped, ask whether the evidence was weak or the deadline had simply passed, and who was holding the complaint during the years it ran down.
DEU.mechanism: A state body with the legal power to place children used it to hand them to known abusers, and the years institutions spent not reporting ran down the legal deadline that would have allowed a prosecution.

FRA.story:
In 2004 the FBI traced a French surgeon, Joël Le Scouarnec, downloading images of children being abused. A court convicted him in 2005 and gave him four months suspended, which means no prison and, in his case, no restriction on practising medicine. Prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities; the regional medical body looked and found no breach in 2006; a warning reached the health ministry in 2007 and produced nothing; and in 2008 a hospital hired him knowing about the conviction. Nothing in the system obliged any of those bodies to tell the next one, so a conviction about pictures of children never became a question about his access to children. Between 1989 and 2014 he abused 299 victims, most of them patients, many under anaesthetic or waking from surgery; more than 250 were under fifteen. He was first convicted of abusing children in 2020 and sentenced in May 2025 to the maximum twenty years.

When the French bishops wanted their own record counted, the commission they set up in 2018 under Jean-Marc Sauvé did not count from church files. Files only hold the complaints an institution agreed to write down, so counting them measures the institution's record-keeping. The commission ran a survey of the general population instead, and in October 2021 estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by clergy and religious between 1950 and 2020, and about 330,000 counting lay staff in church institutions.

Extradition is one country asking another to hand over a person for trial, and the second country can say no. Fr Johannes Rivoire, a French priest of the Oblate order, worked in the Canadian Arctic from 1959 to 1993 and then went home to France. Canada issued a warrant in 1998 and another in 2022; France refused the extradition request, and he died in France in April 2024, never tried. A review commissioned by his own order, by the retired judge André Denis, concluded a month earlier that on the weight of the evidence he had assaulted six Inuit children.

France also moved children as policy. Between 1963 and 1982 the state took about 2,000 children on Réunion who had been made wards of the state and sent them to thinly populated rural departments of mainland France; some were adopted, others were put to work on farms. The National Assembly resolved in 2014 that the state had failed in its moral responsibility to them, and no compensation has been planned.

The French record shows what happens when a warning has no legal duty attached to it: it sits in the file of whoever received it. Read any case here by tracing the warning rather than the crime — who was told, in what year, and what rule said they could keep it to themselves.
FRA.mechanism: Warnings that reached prosecutors, a medical regulator and a ministry with no duty to pass them to the next body, so an offender kept his access to children while the paperwork sat still.

UKR.story:
Ukraine inherited a large system of residential institutions: orphanages, boarding schools and homes for children with disabilities, many of whose residents still have living parents too poor to keep them. A child in one of those buildings has no adult of their own counting the days. Disability Rights International visited 33 of them between 2012 and 2015 and published its findings as No Way Home. The Ukrainian anti-trafficking group La Strada told the investigators that recruiting children out of orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that exploitation inside the institutions usually started at about age 13, often begun by staff. A counter-trafficking coordinator at the International Organization for Migration called the orphanages a direct feeder into trafficking, and said most documented cases began in the vocational schools that leavers are sent on to.

After February 2022 the same absence of a parent made those children movable by a state. Russia's route was paperwork. On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree making it easier to give a Ukrainian child Russian citizenship, which is the step that allows a Russian family to adopt one; Russia then kept a register of families who wanted to and paid them for each adopted child granted citizenship. A new nationality and a new name are what make a child hard to find afterwards: the Ukrainian record and the Russian one no longer describe the same person. Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's children's rights commissioner, said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for re-education. On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and transfer of children. That court has no police force, so a warrant takes effect only if the person travels to a country willing to make the arrest. The UN Secretary-General has verified 122 abducted children; by 2025 two had been reunited with their families and the whereabouts of the rest were unknown.

Inside Ukraine the war moved children again: the 2025 US trafficking report says children evacuated from at least 195 facilities are at high risk, that officials of several state institutions were alleged to be complicit or negligent, and that for the eighth year running no complicit official had been convicted.

Ukraine shows that the same feature makes a child easy to exploit in peace and easy to deport in war: an institution, not a family, holds the papers. When you see a figure like 20,651 deported children, the useful follow-up is not whether the number is right but how many have been traced, and who held legal responsibility for them before they were taken.
UKR.mechanism: Children held by institutions rather than families have nobody to notice them missing, which makes them the first recruits for traffickers in peacetime and the easiest to deport and re-register as another country's citizens in war.

NZL.story:
A child in state care in New Zealand arrived there by someone else's decision: a welfare officer or a court sent them. Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit of Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks given without anaesthetic and painful injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children raped and sexually abused by staff and by adult patients. A hospital converts those acts into treatment: written in a clinical file by a doctor, there is no complaint to pass to police, only a record of care. The psychiatrist in charge, Selwyn Leeks, denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. Because the Crown's own policy would not recognise the lasting harm, survivors went to the UN Committee Against Torture, a body that checks whether a government is keeping a treaty it signed and can issue a finding but impose no penalty. In 2019 it found New Zealand had failed to investigate properly. Police reopened the case in 2020, and in December 2024 the government offered each survivor NZ$150,000 and an apology that used the word torture.

The Royal Commission that found the torture worked differently from a court: instead of counting complaints, which only measures how many people felt able to make one, it estimated across everyone who had passed through care. Its final report, Whanaketia, published on 24 July 2024, put the figure at about 200,000 abused out of roughly 655,000 people in state and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019, with Māori more likely to be abused. It recorded a 2020 church briefing that 14 per cent of Catholic clergy were accused over 1950 to 1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch, run by the St John of God Brothers.

The commission found the church had used psychiatrists' opinions to move abusers into other ministries, where they offended again. A clinical opinion turns a decision about a crime into a decision about a patient, and it gives the bishop who signs the transfer something to point at. Those transfers crossed borders into countries with no inquiry of their own: after allegations in 1977 the St John of God order sent Brother Bernard McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges. The commission recommended an investigation into priests sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations, and a survivor advocate named Fiji as a common destination for clergy transferred from Australia and New Zealand.

New Zealand's lesson is about measurement and about export: a number only appears when someone counts the whole population in care, and a man only disappears from the record when he is sent to a country that is not counting at all. When an institution says an abuser was moved on professional advice, ask who the professional was working for, and whether the new posting was told anything.
NZL.mechanism: Medical authority used twice over: to record the abuse of children in state care as treatment, and to license the transfer of abusers to countries with no inquiry of their own.

LKA.story:
An intercountry adoption rests on a court being satisfied that the mother consents; the receiving country then accepts the court's paper and asks nothing further. So the arrangement can be worked by anyone able to put a woman in front of a judge. Through the 1980s in Sri Lanka, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses bought or took newborn babies and handed them to paid "acting mothers", who appeared in court as birth mothers, and adoption records were widely falsified. Police raided one of these baby farms in 1987 and found 20 newborns and 22 women held in what was described as "prison like conditions", after which Sri Lanka banned foreign adoptions temporarily. About 11,000 children are counted in the case, roughly 4,000 of them sent to the Netherlands and others to Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Germany. The admission came thirty years later: after a Dutch documentary in September 2017, the health minister Rajitha Senaratne said on camera that "there were a lot of baby farms back then" and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. A Dutch commission chaired by Tjibbe Joustra reported in February 2021 that its own government had known of the wrongdoing for years and failed to act, and the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption the same day.

Sri Lanka also sent soldiers. UN peacekeepers stay under the criminal law of the country that sent them, so the UN can do nothing worse than put a soldier on a plane home. The UN's internal oversight office concluded that sexual exploitation and abuse of children by the Sri Lankan contingent in Haiti was "frequent" and occurred "at virtually every location" where it was deployed. In November 2007, 114 of the 950 contingent members were accused and 108 were sent home. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children between 2004 and 2007. At home, authorities judged the acts consensual and nobody was jailed. One victim received a single ex gratia payment in 2016, meaning money handed over without any admission of legal fault.

At a children's home in Vavuniya housing war-affected Tamil children, complaints about the Buddhist monk who ran it reached the National Child Protection Authority, the state body meant to act on exactly those complaints, from 2010. He was arrested in October 2013 only after local child protection officers protested, and that December he was given unconditional bail because the Attorney General's Department, acting on the Authority's instructions, told the court it had no objection.

Sri Lanka's record shows that a document trail can be complete and still be false, and that the body named as a child's protector can be the one arguing for the accused's release. When a country says adoptions from the period were legal, ask who verified that the woman in the courtroom was the mother, and who checks the regulator.
LKA.mechanism: A system that checked documents instead of parentage, so children could be bought and exported legally, and the agencies meant to protect children — a child protection authority at home, a soldier's own courts abroad — acted for the accused instead.

ISR.story:
Extradition — one state handing a person to another for trial — can be stopped by a medical opinion: if psychiatrists judge someone unfit to stand trial, the handover does not happen, and those psychiatrists usually work for the health ministry. In March 2008, after a teacher at the ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School in Melbourne confronted the headmistress, Malka Leifer, about abuse of pupils, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children, and did not tell police. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 covering 74 offences against at least eight pupils, and Israel arrested her that August. Her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals, each resetting the timetable, while Israel's deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, pressured ministry staff to change the psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit. A court found in 2019 that she had faked mental illness. She was extradited on 25 January 2021, convicted by a Melbourne jury on 3 April 2023 of 18 charges including rape, and sentenced to 15 years. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a plea deal in January 2022, resigned from the Knesset in June, and was sentenced to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Israel did extradite a Russian Orthodox priest, Fr Gleb Grozovsky, who fled there in 2013 and was jailed for 14 years in Russia in 2018, so the delay in Leifer's case was not a limit of the system.

An institution can also make a child disappear with a death certificate. Between 1948 and 1954 more than 1,000 families, mostly immigrants from Yemen and dozens from the Balkans, North Africa and elsewhere in the Middle East, took babies to Israeli hospitals, were told the child had died, and were never shown a grave. Many believe the children were given away for adoption. With no body and no burial record, a family can prove neither death nor adoption, and the only evidence is held by the state that wrote the record; three government inquiries since the 1960s concluded that most of the children died of disease and were buried without the parents being informed. On 22 February 2021 the government expressed regret and approved NIS 162 million in compensation — NIS 150,000 for each child whose death was reported to the family at the time, and NIS 200,000 where the fate is unknown. The second, larger payment is the state conceding that some of these children cannot be accounted for.

Israel teaches that a case can be stalled without anyone refusing it: a fitness assessment, repeated hearings, and a file that only the state holds all work by delay rather than denial. When an accused person abroad stays out of reach for years, ask which officials sign the documents that keep them there, and what happened to those officials afterwards.
ISR.mechanism: Delay as protection: a government minister altering psychiatric assessments to keep an accused woman unextraditable, and state records of infant deaths that leave families unable to prove either death or adoption.

CHN.story:
Foreign adoption agencies pay fees to the institution that supplies the child, which means an orphanage with an empty cot has lost money. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought infants from traffickers who brought them up from Guangdong and placed nearly 1,000 of them with families in China and abroad. When it surfaced in 2005, 23 civil officials were fired, three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to between three and 13 years. The orphanages sat inside a programme China had opened in 1992, which sent about 160,000 children abroad and peaked at almost 8,000 to the United States in 2005. Reporting in the New Yorker described a programme that came to rely more and more on abduction and trafficking. On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry ended it, except for adoption by a blood relative or a stepchild.

China is also where several trafficking routes end, and the reason is price. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2019 that women and girls from Myanmar's Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by fighting, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to 13,000, locked up and raped so that they would become pregnant; one survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. Human Rights Watch said authorities on both sides of the border were "looking away", which is what keeps the price low: a buyer who expects no police attention pays nothing for the risk. Brokers sold 629 Pakistani girls and women to Chinese men as brides in 2018 and 2019, and the 2025 US trafficking report describes women and girls from northern Vietnam and Laos taken into China for forced marriage.

A state can also remove children by building the places they will live in. As hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the BBC reported in July 2019, drawing on research by Adrian Zenz, a fast programme of boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitories, including $1.2 billion of spending in southern Xinjiang; in one township more than 400 children had lost both parents to internment or prison. The New York Times reported about 497,000 pupils in such schools, and a Xinjiang propaganda official denied the state was caring for large numbers of parentless children. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here; this is a record of children removed.

The world's figures for online abuse come mostly from the American clearinghouse that receives reports from American platforms, so they measure where those apps are used. In 2025 it logged 9,406 reports for China, a country of about 1.4 billion people, against 1,933,900 for India. Most US platforms are blocked in China, so the counting system cannot see inside it.

China shows that a low number can be a property of the measuring device rather than the country. Where the state owns the orphanages, the courts and the networks, ask who outside the state was ever in a position to check what happened to a particular child.
CHN.mechanism: A state that is the only possible auditor of itself — it ran the orphanages that were paid per child, the border where brides were bought with no enforcement risk, and the networks that keep foreign reporting systems from seeing in.

GRC.story:
A proxy adoption lets the adoptive parents stay at home: a lawyer or agency stands in for them before the court in the child's country, so nobody there ever sees who is receiving the child. Greece used that route heavily. Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many of them described as orphans of the civil war or recorded as born outside marriage, were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures, moving through state institutions and foundling homes and through American agencies including AHEPA. The paperwork was covered by confidentiality, and the practical result was that many of these children grew up with no document proving where they came from — a sealed file cannot be used by the person it describes.

The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s and never carried it out. Without one there is no official account of what happened, so each adoptee has had to establish their own origins alone, from records they were not allowed to see. That changed only on 2 May 2025, when a law recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to the files. One receiving country looked at its own part a month later: Sweden's independent inquiry reported on 2 June 2025 in nearly 1,600 pages, covering 65 years and documenting irregularities and illegalities that Swedish state authorities had some knowledge of.

Greek institutions for children have been examined more recently, and what they show is what staff shortages turn into. In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman, an independent official who can investigate state bodies and publish findings but cannot prosecute, reported on the state care centre at Lechaina, which housed children with disabilities: too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds, and wooden cage beds used because there were not enough staff, with most children receiving no education. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern in 2012, and a BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. No sexual-abuse finding was located at Lechaina; this is a record of neglect and restraint.

Greece shows how long a state can hold a child's own file: fifty years passed between the adoptions and the law that let the adoptees see their records. When a government announces an investigation into something like this, the thing to check later is whether it was ever carried out, and whether the people it concerned were given their papers.
GRC.mechanism: Adoption by proxy plus sealed files: children were sent abroad without anyone in Greece seeing who received them, and the state kept the only proof of their origins for half a century.

GTM.story:
A notary in Guatemala is a private lawyer with the legal power to certify documents. After the civil war ended in 1996, about 98 per cent of adoptions abroad were handled by notaries who took both sides of the transaction — the birth mother's and the adoptive family's — with no court reviewing what they certified, and charged $35,000 or more per child. The only person checking whether a mother had given up her baby freely was the person being paid for the result. Ninety-seven per cent of the children went to the United States, which issued 32,863 visas for children adopted from Guatemala between 1994 and 2014, 4,728 of them in 2007.

That peak year was also the year it stopped. On 11 August 2007 police entered the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua, after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children every day, and found 46 children aged from a few days to three years. Two lawyers who had processed the adoptions were arrested, and the Attorney General, Mario Gordillo, said most of the children lacked proper documents and that his office was checking whether they had been stolen or taken from mothers under coercion. In December Guatemala passed a law meeting the Hague Convention, the treaty that requires a court rather than a paid intermediary to confirm a child is genuinely available for adoption, and from 1 January 2008 it stopped new adoptions to the United States. A commission known as CICIG examined 153 of the old cases in 2010 and found that 78 per cent had broken the law in some way.

Children who stayed behind were held in state homes. About 700 lived at the Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción, built for 500, and most had committed no crime. Girls there protested about overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff, prosecutors recommended closing the place, and in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures — a regional body's request that a government protect people at immediate risk, which that same government has to carry out — citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children out of the home. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police brought a group of girls back and locked them in a room; the next day one of them set a mattress alight, 41 girls died and 15 were injured, and the officers outside did not unlock the door. On 12 August 2025 a judge convicted six former officials, sentencing the former social welfare secretary Carlos Rodas to 25 years and the officer who held the key to 13; the judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses nobody acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.

Guatemala shows what happens when the person who certifies that a child can be adopted is paid by the buyer, and what a warning is worth when the body receiving it has no power to act. When an adoption market is closed down, the questions are where its brokers went and who took charge of the children who were never sold.
GTM.mechanism: Private intermediaries paid per child, certifying their own transactions with no judge looking, and a state home whose documented warnings reached bodies that could only ask the government to act.

JPN.story:
Japanese television needed pop stars, and one agency supplied them. Johnny & Associates could decide which broadcasters got its performers, so a programme that reported on its founder risked losing the acts its schedule depended on. That is how facts stayed public and unused for decades. The earliest cited report about the founder, Johnny Kitagawa, appeared in the weekly Sankei in 1965. In 1999 the magazine Shūkan Bunshun ran a series saying he sexually abused boys who trained at the agency hoping to become singers. Kitagawa sued for defamation and won a judgment in 2002, but a higher court upheld the magazine's reporting on the abuse, reducing the damages in 2003, and the Supreme Court rejected his appeal in 2004. From that point a court had accepted the reporting as substantiated, and Japanese mainstream media still barely covered it; journalists attributed that to the agency's control over bookings. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.

The account only moved in 2023, after a BBC documentary in March and a former trainee's public allegations in April. A UN Human Rights Council working group visited in July. An investigation the agency itself set up concluded on 29 August 2023 that Kitagawa had abused minors who wanted to be pop singers over decades — the BBC puts it at hundreds of boys and young men across a six-decade career. The company admitted it that September and split in two: a new talent agency, and Smile-Up, which pays compensation through a relief committee of three former judges. 478 people came forward, 325 sought compensation and 545 were eventually paid. In March 2024 Smile-Up's chief executive said he believed two more abusers had worked there. Twenty-four years separate the 1999 series from the first official action.

Japan's criminal law also set a time limit on these cases, which matters because people abused as children usually speak much later. A Penal Code reform in June 2023 extended the limitation period for rape from 10 to 15 years and raised the age of consent from 13 to 16. The survivor group Spring said it was not enough.

One case went differently because of who held jurisdiction. In September 1995 three US servicemen based at Camp Hansen on Okinawa abducted and raped a 12-year-old girl. They were tried in a Japanese court rather than sent home to their own, and in 1996 each was sentenced to between six and a half and seven years. The case set off mass protests against the American bases.

Japan shows that publication is not the same as consequence: the Kitagawa allegations were printed, contested in court and upheld, then left alone by everyone who needed the agency's business. When a well-known figure is named and nothing follows, ask which organisations depended on him commercially, and what they would have lost by reporting it.
JPN.mechanism: Commercial dependence as censorship: allegations upheld in court stayed unreported for twenty years because the media needed the accused's talent agency.

KEN.story:
Moving an abandoned child between institutions is an ordinary administrative act with forms to match, and that is what made the trade in Nairobi babies hard to see. BBC Africa Eye spent a year on it and published in November 2020. Reporters found children snatched from homeless mothers on the street and sold for about £350 to £550, and illegal street clinics selling newborns — one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70. At the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, a clinical social worker sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings, about £2,000, and used legitimate transfer paperwork to do it. A sale carried out on the correct form leaves a record that looks like care. The reporters delivered every child they were sold to a children's home. After the story ran, the BBC said the official appeared to have kept his job and the clinic appeared to still be operating.

On the coast the buyers were largely foreign: a 2006 study by UNICEF and the Kenyan government found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of the clients of exploited children there, and Kenyans 38 per cent. What has changed since is the venue. The 2025 US trafficking report cites a 2023 study estimating more than 2,000 children exploited in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and holiday homes rather than hotels. That shift matters because a hotel is licensed, inspected and staffed by people who can be trained to notice a child; a rented villa is none of those things. The report also describes rings bringing girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and says concerns about officials taking part continue with no action reported against any of them. A few offenders answer at home: Keith Morris was jailed in Britain for 18 and a half years over ten offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of only about eight British prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

One widely broadcast Kenyan story was false. In May 2011 the Irish broadcaster RTÉ's documentary "Mission to Prey" accused an Irish priest, Fr Kevin Reynolds, of fathering a child with a minor in Kenya. The allegation was disproved. RTÉ apologised, paid a substantial libel settlement, and its director general called it one of the gravest mistakes the broadcaster had made. Every institution that wants to dismiss a true complaint can now point to it.

Kenya shows a trade that works through correct paperwork and private addresses rather than concealment. When a report describes exploitation moving from hotels into villas, ask who still has the right to walk in and look, and when a story is published, ask whether anyone checked it before it was broadcast.
KEN.mechanism: A trade that runs on legitimate documents and uninspectable premises: official transfer forms used to sell children, and tourist exploitation moving from licensed hotels into private villas.

PER.story:
A religious order is one employer operating in many countries, so moving a man from one country to another is an internal staffing decision and no police force on either side of the border is told. In 1964, in Lima, a Spanish Jesuit named Alfonso Pedrajas abused a minor for the first time. He settled in Bolivia, where he went on to abuse more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools; he confessed to a superior in 1978 and the superior covered it up. Peru has been the receiving end of the same arrangement: in 2010 a Marist Brother in Chile, Abel Pérez, told his superiors he had abused minors, and the Marist Brothers transferred him to Peru. Nothing in either move required a lie, because nobody outside the order had to be consulted.

Peru's clearest reckoning so far was paid for by the organisation under examination. In 2016 the Catholic movement Sodalitium Christianae Vitae commissioned an inquiry into its own founder, Luis Figari, and the report that followed in February 2017 found that he had sexually abused at least one minor and others. An inquiry of that kind picks its own investigators, sets its own limits and decides what to publish; it cannot compel anyone to give evidence, and it has no obligation to hand what it learns to prosecutors.

Current exploitation in Peru is organised around places that are hard to reach. The 2025 US trafficking report says tourists from the United States and Europe exploit children in Cusco, Lima and the Peruvian Amazon, and that in Loreto criminal groups take foreign tourists by boat to remote venues on the Amazon River. Distance is the protection: a venue two hours upriver cannot be inspected without a boat, and a witness cannot walk out of it. Peruvian, Venezuelan and Bolivian women and girls are drawn to mining and logging camps, and the Venezuelan group Tren de Aragua has reportedly moved trafficking victims from the Colombian border city of Cúcuta into Peru. Peruvian courts convicted 59 traffickers in 2024, two police officers were charged with crimes against trafficking victims, and the report calls corruption a significant concern.

Peru teaches that a border is only an obstacle to the people investigating, not to the institution doing the moving. When a church or an order announces its own investigation, ask who appointed the investigators and whether the findings went to the police; when exploitation is described in remote places, ask who is physically able to go and check.
PER.mechanism: A religious order moving accused men across borders as a staffing matter, and an institution investigating itself, with today's exploitation placed where no inspector can physically arrive.

SDN.story:
In a war there is usually nobody for a family to report a rape to, because the men who did it are the armed force holding the area. The counting is therefore done from outside. An independent international fact-finding mission for Sudan interviewed survivors who had reached somewhere safe, and separately the UN Secretary-General publishes cases his staff have been able to corroborate, which they call verified. Both methods depend on access, so their numbers are a floor rather than a total.

The mission found that rape and gang rape were widespread in Sudan after the war began in 2023, carried out mostly by men in the uniform of the Rapid Support Forces and allied militias, with some cases by the Sudanese Armed Forces. Victims included girls as young as eight. It also found that the RSF's abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes amounted to sexual slavery — a specific crime in international law, where holding the person is itself the offence, which matters because it attaches responsibility to the commanders who ran the places where they were held. The Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023, 57 of those cases by the RSF, and against 74 children in 2024, 54 by the RSF and nine by militias affiliated with it, and the UN now lists the RSF for the rape and abduction of children. That listing is a formal naming in an annual report; it carries no penalty of its own.

Soldiers from a neighbouring country appear in the same records. The UN attributed four of 35 verified cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 in Sudan to the Chadian National Army, and verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by that army in Chad's own Lac Province in 2022. A foreign army answers to its own command, not to Sudanese courts.

Sudan is also where children from elsewhere end up: the 2025 US trafficking report says Ethiopian girls are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes controlled with drugs, and that reports of officials taking part continued. Nobody is measuring the online side at all; the Middle East and North Africa region has no representative survey data on technology-facilitated exploitation of children.

Sudan shows what happens when the accused is the authority: the only counting is done by people who were not allowed in. When you read a verified figure such as 114 girls, treat it as the number investigators could reach, and ask which court could ever try a commander for the rest.
SDN.mechanism: When the armed force in control is the one committing the abuse, there is no authority to report to, and the record consists only of what outside investigators could reach.

DOM.story:
A papal nuncio is the Pope's ambassador to a country, and like any ambassador he can be recalled by the government that sent him. That is how one case left the Dominican Republic. Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, a Polish cleric, arrived in Santo Domingo as nuncio in 2008. In August 2013, amid allegations that he had abused minors, the Vatican called him back to Rome. Dominican prosecutors opened their criminal investigation on 4 September 2013, after he had gone, and prosecutors with no suspect in the country have nothing to arrest. The Holy See later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was removed from the priesthood in June 2014; in June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor charged him with abusing children in the Dominican Republic between 2008 and 2013 and with possessing abuse images. He was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before any trial.

A priest from the same country shows that leaving need not end a case. Fr Wojciech Gil, who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was suspended in May 2013 and went home to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic — meaning no Dominican request could have compelled his return. Poland prosecuted him anyway: police arrested him in February 2014 using evidence gathered in the Dominican Republic, and on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors there between 2009 and 2013 and two in Poland. The same flight home produced two different endings, and the difference was the home country's willingness to act.

The north coast draws offenders who travel. American men have been prosecuted under the PROTECT Act, a US law that allows citizens to be tried at home for abusing children abroad, over boys and girls in Puerto Plata and Sosúa, and US and Dominican agents have run joint operations in the tourist towns. After the 2010 earthquake in Haiti, members of a US group calling itself New Life Children's Refuge tried to take 33 children across the border into the Dominican Republic.

The Dominican record is about timing and jurisdiction: in both clerical cases the accused was out of the country before local police could act, and only one was convicted, by his own country. When an accused official leaves a country just before an investigation opens, ask who arranged the departure and who was told about it first.
DOM.mechanism: Diplomatic recall and a flight home before an investigation opens, leaving prosecution entirely to the accused man's own country.

CZE.story:
A suspended sentence means the court records a conviction and the prison term but does not make the person serve it, so long as he stays out of trouble. In 2000 and 2001 a Czech court found Fr František Merta, a priest of the Archdiocese of Olomouc, guilty of abusing more than 20 boys, and gave him two years suspended. The archbishop, Jan Graubner, is alleged to have failed to report him and to have moved him from parish to parish as problems arose. A move of that kind works because a parish knows only what it is told: the complaint stays with the congregation that made it, and the new one starts from nothing. The suspended sentence left the only real question — whether he would be near children again — to the institution that had been moving him.

Czechia also appears as a place where abuse images were produced. A Czech photographer and a Swedish partner distributed images of about 70 children to buyers in the European Union and Canada until Europol announced the network dismantled. That split is the reason such businesses last: the people photographing children are in one country and the customers in several others, so no single police force ever sees more than a fragment, and the case only exists when forces agree to pool what they have.

The country's history also includes occupation. Nazi Germany seized children it judged "racially valuable" in the territories it held, kept them in Lebensborn and other homes, and placed them with German families under new identities; DW cites estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children taken and forcibly Germanized. At the Nuremberg trial of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, which ran the programme, 13 of the 14 officials charged were convicted on 10 March 1948 and one was acquitted; the head of the office, Ulrich Greifelt, was given life.

What the Czech record shows is how little a conviction settles on its own: a court can find a man guilty of abusing more than 20 children and leave him in the hands of his employer. When you read that someone received a suspended sentence, the question is what he was permitted to do the following week, and who decided it.
CZE.mechanism: A conviction that changed nothing: a suspended sentence left the decision about an abuser's access to children with the employer that had been moving him between parishes.

NER.story:
Before the UN counts a child as abducted in a war, its monitors have to corroborate the report and then attribute it to someone: a named armed group, a government force, or, when they cannot establish who did it, to unidentified perpetrators. In Niger in 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 202 children, 102 of them girls. It attributed 35 to the armed group known as JAS, two to ISWAP and two to ISGS, and 163 — the great majority — to perpetrators it could not identify. It also verified sexual violence against five girls that year. In 2023 it verified sexual violence against eight girls, one of those cases committed by Niger's own security forces.

That large unidentified column is the mechanism worth understanding. The children are confirmed gone, but with no party attached there is no commander to name, no force a government or donor can be pressed to discipline, and nothing to add to the annual list of parties that abduct children. Accountability runs through attribution, so a case without a named perpetrator stops at the counting stage.

Everything outside the conflict monitoring is simply unmeasured. The estimates used for online exploitation of children come from representative population surveys, and the 2026 Childlight update rests on surveys from only 60 countries; West and Central Africa is among the regions without them, so no figure exists for how many children in Niger are exploited that way.

Niger teaches that a record can confirm a harm and still identify nobody, and that a country can be nearly blank on a map because no survey has ever been run there. When you see a number for a conflict, check how much of it is attributed, and when you see no number at all, ask who would have had to pay for the survey.
NER.mechanism: Accountability runs through attribution, so most of Niger's verified child abductions — assigned to unidentified perpetrators — end at the counting stage, and nothing outside conflict monitoring is measured at all.

BOL.story:
When a priest confesses abuse to his superior, the superior decides whether anyone outside the order ever learns of it. In 1964, in Lima, the Spanish Jesuit Alfonso Pedrajas abused a minor for the first time. He then settled in Bolivia, where he abused more than 80 minors at Jesuit schools. He confessed to a superior in 1978, and the superior covered it up rather than reporting him, so the only account of what he had done stayed in the order's own hands while he kept working with children. Bolivia did not import a stranger; it received a man whose employer already knew.

The exploitation described in Bolivia now works on a different geography. The 2025 US trafficking report says foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in the north of La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque, in Santa Cruz, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It also reports that the production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, in some cases involving the children's parents. That arrangement splits the crime in two: the child is abused where they live, and the payment comes from a buyer in another country, so local police see no customer and the buyer's police see no child. Bolivian women and girls are also exploited in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru, and the Venezuelan group Tren de Aragua is reported to be involved in trafficking in the country.

Bolivia shows two kinds of distance doing the same work. A religious order's internal confession keeps a case from ever reaching a prosecutor, and an internet payment keeps the buyer out of the jurisdiction where the child is. When abuse is described in a remote community visited by foreigners, ask which adult there has any authority to intervene, and whether the visitor's home country prosecutes its citizens for what they do abroad.
BOL.mechanism: Distance used as cover: an order's internal confession kept a case from any prosecutor, and online payment keeps the buyer in a different jurisdiction from the child.

IRQ.story:
What distinguishes a planned campaign from scattered violence is logistics, and in northern Iraq the logistics are documented. Islamic State fighters attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis — members of a religious minority — by bus and truck in an organised way to holding sites: Tal Afar, Baaj, and in Mosul both Badoush prison and the Galaxy wedding hall. From there women and girls were taken on to Raqqa in Syria and sold. Transport, holding places and markets all require people assigned to run them, which is what makes this a policy rather than a series of attacks.

The finding came from the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria, a body of investigators appointed to gather evidence rather than to try anyone. Its June 2016 report, "They came to destroy", concluded that Islamic State had committed genocide against the Yazidis, that women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and that boys were taken into its training camps. A commission's finding is not a verdict and sentences nobody; its value is that the evidence survives for courts that may come later.

At the time of that report, more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, most of them in Syria, and thousands remain missing. That number is a snapshot of people in captivity on a particular date, not a total of everyone taken, and as the territory changed hands the captives in it were dispersed, which is why the missing are now scattered across more than one country. Nothing comparable exists for the rest of child exploitation in Iraq: the Middle East and North Africa region has no representative survey data on technology-facilitated abuse.

Iraq's record shows the sale of children organised as administration, with vehicles, buildings and buyers. When a figure like 3,200 is quoted, ask what date it describes and who is searching now, because a number counting people still held becomes less accurate every year it is repeated.
IRQ.mechanism: The sale of children run as organised administration — transport, holding sites and markets — recorded by investigators who can establish facts but cannot convict anyone.

LBR.story:
A private orphanage is a business with two sources of income: donations, and the fees paid when a child is placed with a family abroad. Both depend on having children in the building. When Liberia's civil war ended in 2003, the number of private orphanages went from 40 to 120, and the UN mission in the country found orphanages that were run for profit and had no accreditation at all. What those homes contained became clear in 2005, when the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their own families. Nearly all of them had parents.

A 2007 report by UNICEF and the adoption agency Holt International found that many Liberian children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises made to birth parents — the usual version being that the child will be fed and schooled and will come home. A parent who agrees to that has not agreed to an adoption, but the paperwork says otherwise by the time it reaches the other country. The United States issued 1,553 visas for children adopted from Liberia between 1994 and 2014, with 353 in 2006 alone, and Canada stopped Liberian adoptions with a moratorium.

Almost nothing else about Liberia is measured. Figures for online exploitation of children come from representative population surveys, and the 2026 Childlight update draws on surveys from only 60 countries; West and Central Africa has none, so no estimate exists for Liberia.

Liberia shows that an orphanage boom after a war is a supply response, not a rise in orphans. When you read that a country's orphanages tripled, the questions are how many of the children have living parents, what those parents were told, and who receives the money at the moment a child is placed abroad.
LBR.mechanism: Orphanages run as businesses that need children, recruiting them from living parents with false promises so they can be placed abroad for a fee.

CMR.story:
UN monitors in a conflict do not publish what they are told; they publish what they can corroborate and attach to a named party. In Cameroon in 2023 they verified sexual violence against 17 girls, attributing ten of those cases to the Cameroon Armed Forces, the country's own army, six to perpetrators they could not identify and one to the armed group JAS. In 2024 they verified sexual violence against six girls, one of those cases by the armed forces, and the abduction of 50 children.

The majority attribution to the national army is what a reader should sit with, because of who would have to act on it. A soldier is investigated in the first instance by his own force, under officers whose own standing is affected by the result, and the UN body that recorded these cases has no power to charge anyone or to require that the state does. The sources here record what was verified; they do not record any prosecution, so a reader cannot tell from them whether any of the ten cases went anywhere.

Outside the conflict reporting there is no measurement at all. Estimates of online exploitation of children rest on representative population surveys, and West and Central Africa has none, so no figure exists for how many children in Cameroon are abused that way.

Cameroon shows a record where the accused and the only available investigator belong to the same institution. When verified cases are attributed to a national army, look for whether any case reached a court, and remember that a UN verification is a finding about evidence, not the start of a prosecution.
CMR.mechanism: Most verified cases attributed to the national army, leaving the accused institution as the only body able to investigate, with the UN able to record but not compel.

JEY.story:
Jersey is a small island that governs itself, which means the authority running the children's homes also writes the child-welfare law, employs the inspectors and oversees the police. Between 2007 and 2010 Jersey's police ran Operation Rectangle, an investigation centred on a former children's home called Haut de la Garenne. An Independent Jersey Care Inquiry followed — a panel appointed from outside the island's government, able to take evidence in public — and it heard from about 450 people connected with the care system since 1945 before reporting in July 2017.

It found that the States of Jersey, the island's government, had been "an ineffectual and neglectful substitute parent", and that the island's child-welfare law was decades behind. That second finding matters more than it sounds. A care worker's duties — when a child must be moved out of a placement, what has to be reported and to whom — come from statute, so an old statute can leave a worker who did nothing in breach of no rule, and leave a department with nothing to enforce. The inquiry also found that the authorities had failed to build a culture of transparency, which fed beliefs that officials were colluding and covering up, and that a "small island culture" had never been countered. It recommended that the Haut de la Garenne buildings be demolished, and the Chief Minister, Ian Gorst, apologised: "We failed children who needed our care."

The finding that mattered most for children at the time was not about the past. The inquiry said that some children in care on the island might still be at risk, which is what an inquiry can establish and then leave with the same government to fix.

Jersey shows how a jurisdiction small enough that everyone knows each other can run its own care system with no outside check, and how out-of-date law protects the adults rather than the children. When an inquiry reports on a place like that, read the part about present-day risk first, and ask who, from outside, is now able to inspect.
JEY.mechanism: A self-governing island where the care provider, the lawmaker and the inspectorate are the same authority, operating under child-welfare law decades out of date.

TWN.story:
Most trafficking takes a child who already exists. One operation in Bangkok worked the other way round: it took orders first. In February 2011 Thai police entered two houses in the city and freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, whose passports had been confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that was taking orders from childless couples for newborns. Four of the women said they had been tricked into coming, and Thailand's health minister said some appeared to have been raped. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking.

Two details explain how it held together. The confiscated passports were the lock: a foreign woman without her documents cannot leave the country or walk into a police station without putting herself at risk of arrest. And because each baby was made to fill an order, there was no family searching for a missing child afterwards and no earlier paperwork to contradict — the birth itself generates the first record, and whoever is present at it controls what that record says.

Taiwan also sends children abroad through regular adoption: 4,289 between 2003 and 2022, and that route remains open. Most of the sending countries on this map were closed after an inquiry found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. A country still open has not had that inquiry, which can mean the practice there is sound or only that nobody has examined it.

Taiwan's case is a reminder that demand can be met by production rather than abduction, which leaves a cleaner paper trail than a stolen child does. When an adoption or surrogacy route is described as legal and still running, ask who verifies where each child came from, what was paid, and to whom.
TWN.mechanism: Babies produced to order rather than taken: held birth mothers with confiscated passports, and a first record of the child created by the people selling it.

PNG.story:
Papua New Guinea is on this map because of an inquiry held somewhere else. In 2024 New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care found that the Catholic Church there had transferred abusers into other ministries rather than reporting them, and it recommended a separate investigation into Catholic priests who had been sent to Papua New Guinea after allegations were made against them. The commission did not say how many priests were sent, and nothing in these sources records what happened after they arrived.

That gap is the mechanism, and it follows from how a transfer works. The decision is made inside the institution, in the country where the complaint was raised. No charge was brought, so no police force has a file to pass on. The receiving parish is told that a priest is being posted to it, which is an ordinary event, and the people there have no reason and no means to ask what else is in his record. Unless the receiving country runs an inquiry of its own, nobody in it ever assembles the information that would reveal the pattern — so a mark on Papua New Guinea records a decision taken in New Zealand, not a count of what was done to children here.

What this teaches is that the destination of a transfer is usually the part nobody investigates: the sending country eventually examines itself, while the children in the receiving country stay outside everyone's remit. The questions worth asking are where each of those priests was posted, who in Papua New Guinea was ever told why they came, and whether any body there has the authority to look.
PNG.mechanism: The destination of an institutional transfer, where no charge, file or inquiry follows the man, so the only record of him exists in the country that sent him away.

KGZ.story:
A government can stop foreign adoptions without explaining itself. A suspension is an administrative act: new cases are not processed, and no court finding, published report or named wrongdoer is required for it. Kyrgyzstan suspended intercountry adoption in 2009, and in April 2010 the US State Department issued an alert so that American families would know. The sources here do not say what prompted the decision, and no individual case from Kyrgyzstan is recorded on this map.

What gives the suspension its meaning is the sequence it belongs to. Intercountry adoption has moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed: South Korea, Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2007 and 2008, Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia, which banned it in 2018. Each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. The demand does not close with them. The families waiting and the agencies arranging the placements remain, so a country that stops is usually followed by a country that starts, and the pipeline reappears somewhere with weaker checks.

Kyrgyzstan therefore sits on this map as a stop without a stated finding. When a country suspends adoptions, the two things worth finding out are what its officials had discovered — a suspension with no published reason leaves that permanently unclear — and which country the same agencies began working in next.
KGZ.mechanism: A suspension with no published finding — the adoption pipeline closing in one country and reopening in the next, with the reason never recorded.

GUM.story:
People abused as children usually say so decades later, by which time the legal deadline for suing has normally expired, and an expired claim cannot be heard however strong it is. Some governments have reopened that right by passing a window. In 2016 Guam, a US territory in the Pacific, opened a permanent one, meaning a survivor there can sue however long ago the abuse happened. Claims against the island's Catholic archdiocese then rose to nearly 280.

On 15 and 16 January 2019 the archdiocese filed for bankruptcy. That filing changes the game rather than ending it. All the individual lawsuits stop; every claim is pooled into one court process and settled together out of whatever assets the court recognises, which means the amount is set by the institution's balance sheet instead of by what a jury might award one survivor. Claimants also give up the trial itself, and with it the sworn testimony and internal documents a trial would have brought into the open. The archdiocese's plan in January 2020 offered $21 million against those claims, and it sold a property in Yona for $6.1 million.

The man at the centre of the island's cases was dealt with by his church rather than a court: the former archbishop, Anthony Apuron, was found guilty in a canonical trial in 2018 and 2019. A canonical trial is held under church law and can remove a cleric from office, but it cannot imprison anyone or award a survivor anything. Guam's sequence is the American one in miniature: from 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

What Guam shows is that lifting a deadline and getting compensation are two different fights, and the second one is decided in a bankruptcy court. When a diocese files soon after a window opens, divide the offer by the number of claims, and ask what the claimants had to give up — usually a public trial — to receive it.
GUM.mechanism: Bankruptcy as the answer to a lifted deadline: claims pooled, the payout set by the institution's assets, and the trial that would have produced documents given up.

GHA.story:
Nothing on this map is recorded for Ghana, and the reason is the method behind every figure on it. The only reliable way to find out how many children in a country have been sexually exploited is to ask a representative sample of the population directly, under conditions that let people answer honestly. Police figures cannot do that job, because they count the cases someone chose to report to an institution, which in most places is a small fraction. A survey of that kind needs money, a trained field team, ethical approval and a government willing to let researchers ask children and young adults about their own lives.

Where that work has not been paid for, a country has no number. Childlight, the research centre that assembles these studies, built its 2026 update from representative surveys in only 60 countries, and West and Central Africa has none covering technology-facilitated exploitation. Ghana is in that gap.

The effect runs the other way too, into the world totals. A global estimate assembled from 60 countries has to extend what it found in those places across the rest, so every region without surveys is represented by figures borrowed from somewhere else. The regions with the most research end up looking like the regions with the most abuse, because they are the only ones measured.

Ghana's blank is a statement about budgets and permissions, not about children. The question to put to any global figure is which countries it actually measured, and for a country like Ghana, who would have to fund and approve a survey before it could ever appear.
GHA.mechanism: The silence of an unmeasured country: prevalence figures exist only where a survey was funded and permitted, and global totals extend the measured countries' numbers over the unmeasured ones.

GNQ.story:
Three separate machines produce almost everything known about child exploitation worldwide, and Equatorial Guinea feeds none of them. The first is the population survey: researchers ask a representative sample of people directly, which requires a funder, a field team and a government's permission. Childlight, the centre that gathers those surveys, had representative data from only 60 countries for its 2026 update, and West and Central Africa has none on technology-facilitated abuse. The second is government self-reporting: the UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied data for 2023, because each country decides for itself whether to submit any. The third is platform reporting, where internet companies pass on what they detect — which depends entirely on whether the people in a country use the services that report.

A country that takes part in none of the three produces no record at all, so nothing appears against it. On a map like this it can only be coloured by estimate: a figure inferred from the countries that were measured, rather than counted here.

That is a different statement from safety. An absence of data means no one has asked, no one has submitted, and no one was monitoring the platforms being used. The thing worth asking about Equatorial Guinea is which of the three mechanisms could realistically be made to work there — who could run a survey, who would have to approve it, and whether the government would publish what it found.
GNQ.mechanism: A country absent from all three counting systems — population surveys, government returns to the UN, and platform reporting — can only be filled in by estimate.

JOR.story:
A country's public record of child abuse is made by two things: the cases that reach police or the press, and the inquiries that go looking for the rest. An inquiry matters because it has powers an ordinary investigation does not — it can call for institutional files, take evidence in public, and ask people who never went to the police to come forward — which is how private knowledge becomes a public count. Without one, the record holds only what someone already chose to report.

Jordan has no documented case on this map, and no survey either. Childlight, the research centre that assembles studies of child sexual exploitation, had representative surveys from only 60 countries for its 2026 update, and the Middle East and North Africa region has none covering technology-facilitated abuse. Government reporting has similar holes: the UN's 2024 global trafficking report covered 156 countries, yet only 72 of them supplied data for 2023.

So the map colours Jordan by estimate, which is a number worked out from countries that were measured and applied here for want of anything better. Reading that as low prevalence would be reading the budget of the research field rather than the lives of children.

Jordan's entry shows what a record looks like when nothing has been built to collect one. When a country appears clean, check whether anyone has ever held an inquiry with power to compel documents, or asked a representative sample of young people anything at all.
JOR.mechanism: No inquiry with power to compel documents and no population survey, so the record holds only what someone already chose to report.

QAT.story:
Asking children about sexual abuse requires permission. A prevalence survey — the method that produces the only trustworthy national figures — needs a funder, an ethics approval, interviewers trained to handle disclosures, and a government willing to let researchers put those questions to its young people and willing to see the answers published. Each of those is a point at which the study can simply not happen, and when it does not happen the country has no measurement, only whatever cases reached police or reporters.

For Qatar, this map holds no documented case. Childlight, the research centre that pools these studies, worked from representative surveys in only 60 countries for its 2026 update, and the Middle East and North Africa region has none on technology-facilitated exploitation. The other main sources have the same structure: governments choose whether to report to the UN, and only 72 of the 156 countries in its 2024 trafficking report supplied data for 2023.

What that leaves is an estimate: a figure derived from the countries where the work was done, applied to the ones where it was not. It is a placeholder for an unknown, and it should be read as one.

Qatar sits here as an example of the permission problem rather than a finding about Qatari children. When you see a country with no cases recorded, ask who inside it has ever been allowed to collect data on children, who outside it has tried, and what happened to the request.
QAT.mechanism: Measurement depends on permission: without a funded and government-approved survey of young people, a country has no figure and is filled in from elsewhere.

TKM.story:
Most of the world's count of online child abuse material comes from one place. American technology companies are required to report what they find to a national clearinghouse in the United States, which passes each report to the country the material appears to come from. This means the figures are a map of where American platforms are used, as much as a map of where children are harmed. In 2025 that system logged 591 reports for Turkmenistan.

Several things can make a number that small. The platforms doing the reporting may hardly be used in a country; the people there may use services that detect and report nothing; and a report only lands on a country when the technical details allow it to be located at all — in 2025, 14 per cent of the system's 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country. North Korea, with no open internet, generated 12.

Turkmenistan has no case recorded on this map and no survey behind it, so it is coloured by estimate: a value inferred from countries that have been measured. A reader who treats 591 as a measure of harm is reading the reach of a handful of companies.

Turkmenistan shows that a reporting system can only see the services that participate in it. When a country's report count is tiny, the useful questions are which apps people there actually use and whether any of those companies report anything, before asking anything about the children.
TKM.mechanism: A report count that measures the reach of American platforms rather than the amount of abuse, leaving countries outside those services nearly invisible.
